newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Welteke says EMU goals key to public trust.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Welteke says EMU goals key to public trust.

text.p: Any softening of the entry criteria for Europe's monetary union could harm public trust in the Euro and would be opposed by the Bundesbank, central bank council member Ernst Welteke said on Thursday.
"We do not want any weakening of the Maastricht criteria," Welteke told reporters after giving a speech on monetary union in his home town of Korbach, in northern Hesse.

"We want a stable currency union for a stable Euro. We have such a high mass of convergence in the centre of Europe. We must do all we can to protect that," Welteke, who heads the Hesse regional central bank, added.

European countries have been reshaping their economies for the last five years in a bid to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation and budgets laid down in the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union.

Welteke warned that any attempt to loosen the entry criteria, or push back the 1999 launch date for the new currency, the Euro, would trigger a public outcry and a turbulent response in financial markets.
"If we move the criteria we would lose everybody's trust," he told reporters.

Asked to comment on a report carried in a German newspaper today suggesting that there were differences between Bonn and the Bundesbank on how monetary union should proceed, Welteke declined to comment specifically.

Having returned from the United States this morning -- after attending international meetings in Washington last week -- Welteke said he had not seen the article in question. But he added that within the Bundesbank itself there was certainly a common view held by all.
"We are very homogeneous (within the Bundesbank). We want stable criteria," he said.

The article, in the German weekly Die Zeit, drew on various comments made by Bundesbank and government officials in recent weeks in a bid to demonstrate that the Bundesbank was unhappy with progress with a planned stability pact for public budgets.

European finance ministers agreed on the broad outlines of the stability pact -- intended to ensure fiscal discipline within monetary union -- at a meeting in Dublin in late September, but they have yet to fill in the details.
Asked about progress in setting up the pact, which was originally proposed by German finance minister Theo Waigel, Welteke said: "It is going in the right direction."
His comment echoed a remark made by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer immediately after the Dublin meeting.
Welteke, who said earlier in his speech that European monetary union should start on time in 1999, warned against anybody considering a delay in the launch of the new currency.

"We must ask ourselves what would happen if there were no monetary union," he said in response to a question from the audience. "One must ask if it is democratic for other countries not to have control over their own currencies and how long they would put up with the Bundesbank's strength."
But although monetary union would bring huge advantages for the Euro area, it would also bring new challenges.
Increased economic convergence after monetary union meant that a unified capital gains tax and value added tax would be needed throughout the area.

And Germany, already suffering from high jobless rates, would face its own problems. High labour costs in the domestic economy meant Germany would be at a competitive disadvantage unless productivity increased.
"Then employment would rise," he warned.
